name: Indian independence movement
scope: The political programme and ideas of the movement to end British rule in India, c. 1885-1947, as Britannica and the Congress's own declarations present it: the Indian National Congress from its moderate reformism (Naoroji, Gokhale) through the Swadeshi 'extremists' (Tilak) and Gandhi's non-violent mass campaigns to the Purna Swaraj declaration of 1930, the Quit India resolution of 1942 and the socialist and militant currents (Nehru, Bose). Its aims are self-rule, economic independence from British exploitation, and a secular, democratic, republican state. It excludes the post-1947 Indian state and Congress governments, Gandhi's own philosophy (reserved for Gandhism), Hindu nationalism (Hindutva), the Muslim League's Pakistan movement, and the events as history (dates, battles, casualties).

summary: The Indian independence movement (c. 1885-1947) sought an end to British rule, moving from the moderates' constitutional reform and 'drain of wealth' critique through swadeshi self-reliance and Gandhi's non-violent non-cooperation and civil disobedience to the demand for Purna Swaraj (complete independence) in 1930 and Quit India in 1942. Its declarations present British rule as economically, politically and culturally ruinous and an affront to the Indian people's right to freedom. Its leaders also held that independence was a step toward ending poverty and inequality of opportunity, and a militant, socialist wing under Bose stood beside the Congress mainstream.

notes: Themes searched: government, economy, society, world, liberty, means (Britannica pages on the movement, Congress, Quit India, Swadeshi and six leaders; the Purna Swaraj declaration; Nehru's Tryst speech). The sources state the movement's aims and methods but little on most test statements, so most are null. The movement spans moderates, extremists, Gandhian non-violence and Bose's militancy, hence 0 on political violence. Gandhi's own writings belong to Gandhism and were not used.
